ambiguities.description: The word 'plan' is used for three distinct concepts: PricePlan (billing artefact), FeatureBundle (product feature set), and a sales-negotiated deal ('third thing a plan') that Priya says is a different meeting. The sales-deal concept is not modeled here -- should it be captured elsewhere?

source_references.excerpt: Tom: We've got two things both called plan, and the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated, which frequently matches neither.

ambiguities.description: Account closure and reopening: if the same company returns, a new account/account number is issued and treated as a new customer, losing history. Is 'Company' a separate concept worth modeling, or is this explicitly out of scope?

source_references.excerpt: Priya: Yes. Six digits, sequential, never reused. If an account closes and the same company comes back, they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting.

ambiguities.description: Paused is described as a separate boolean flag on Subscription that overlaps confusingly with Status, causing bugs where paused subscriptions are returned by 'active' queries. Should Paused be modeled as a formal attribute/constraint, and does it interact with Status in a way that needs an exclusion or subset constraint?

source_references.excerpt: Priya: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag. ... Priya: It behaves like a status but it isn't one, it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs. If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too.

ambiguities.description: The commercial policy for mid-term cancellation of annual subscriptions (run to term vs prorated refund vs credit) is explicitly undecided and parked. Manual credits exist outside the subscription system. Should a Refund or Credit concept be modeled once policy is decided?

source_references.excerpt: Facilitator: Then I'm parking it explicitly. What happens commercially when an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term -- run to term, prorated refund, or credit -- is undecided.

ambiguities.description: Subscription has both a denormalised 'current price plan' field (maintained by the change process) and the full PlanChange history. If they disagree, the change history wins and current plan is considered a bug. This suggests CurrentPricePlan is derived/maintained data rather than an independently assertable fact -- should the identifier fact type 'Subscription has PricePlan' be treated as derived rather than a base fact, similar to MRR?

source_references.excerpt: Priya: No, Sam, it does have a current plan field. The changes are the history, but there's a denormalised current plan on the record. ... Priya: Correct. And if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.

ambiguities.description: A fourth product is 'in discovery' meaning the value constraint on ProductCode (CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT) is expected to change soon. Should the model treat product codes as an open enumeration rather than a fixed value constraint?

source_references.excerpt: Tom: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT. ... Tom: Fixed today. There's a fourth in discovery, but I'm not going to pretend I know what it is.

ambiguities.description: No explicit identifier was given for Contact/Email -- Priya mentions 'Email is on the contact, not the account' but Contact is not otherwise defined. Should Contact be modeled as an entity type with its own identification scheme?

source_references.excerpt: Priya: Company name absolutely not, we have four accounts called "Acme." Email is on the contact, not the account.

object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: The customer entity in the system; everything hangs off it. Identified by account number.

source_references.excerpt: Priya: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off.

object_types.name: AccountNumber
object_types.definition: Six-digit, sequential, never-reused identifier for an Account.

source_references.excerpt: Priya: Yes. Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: The agreement that an account pays a given amount on a given cycle for a given product/plan. Identified by subscription ID.

source_references.excerpt: Priya: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID.

object_types.name: SubscriptionId
object_types.definition: Generated unique identifier for a Subscription, prefixed with SUB.

source_references.excerpt: Priya: Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: One of the company's offerings, e.g. CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT. Identified by product code.

source_references.excerpt: Tom: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.
Tom: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: PricePlan
object_types.definition: The billing artefact that says what the customer pays and how often; generates the invoice line. Identified by plan code.

source_references.excerpt: Priya: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: PlanCode
object_types.definition: Code identifying a PricePlan, e.g. CORE-MO-49.

source_references.excerpt: CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: What the customer gets: a feature bundle such as Starter, Professional, Enterprise, defining seats, API access, SSO, etc. Identified by name.

source_references.excerpt: Tom: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle -- how many seats, whether they get the API, whether they get SSO. It's the thing on the pricing page.

object_types.name: FeatureBundleName
object_types.definition: The unique name of a FeatureBundle, e.g. Starter, Professional, Enterprise.

source_references.excerpt: Tom: Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me. ... Tom: Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: PlanChange
object_types.definition: A record of a change to a subscription's price plan, with an effective date, request date, and requester. Identified by change ID.

source_references.excerpt: Priya: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date, and the subscription's current plan is derived from the change history.
Priya: It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: StartDate
object_types.definition: The date a subscription begins; always present.

source_references.excerpt: Priya: Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: EndDate
object_types.definition: The date a subscription ends; present only for fixed-term subscriptions or after cancellation.

source_references.excerpt: Priya: An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled. A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front, that's usually an enterprise deal.

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: How often the subscription is billed: monthly or annual.

source_references.excerpt: Priya: Monthly or annual. ... Priya: Never neither. Every subscription has exactly one billing period.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStatus
object_types.definition: The current lifecycle status of a subscription: trialing, active, past due, or cancelled.

source_references.excerpt: Priya: Trialing, active, past due, cancelled. ... Priya: Exactly one, yes.

object_types.name: EffectiveDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a plan change takes effect (may differ from the date the change was requested).

source_references.excerpt: Priya: Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.

object_types.name: Requester
object_types.definition: The person who requested a plan change.
